Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the InnoMed Devices Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone. Please note, this call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements, including expectations regarding our future performance, business outlook, and financial results. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Joining me on today's call are Alex Rivera, CEO; Michael Chen, CFO; Dr. Lena Novak, Chief Technology Officer; and Tom Hargrove, Chief Commercial Officer.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. InnoMed Devices delivered strong results this quarter, driven by increasing adoption of our innovative medical devices and strategic partnerships.

Today, I will cover five key aspects of our performance:
1. Impact of pricing and cost management initiatives
2. Gross margin trends and supply chain commentary
3. Inventory management and working capital optimization
4. New product launches and contribution to growth
5. FDA approvals and CE marks obtained

Michael will then provide a more detailed review of our financials. After that, we'll open the call for your questions.

Now, let's get started with the impact of our pricing and cost management initiatives. Michael, please provide the details here.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. As we dive into the financials, one of the key drivers behind our strong performance this quarter has been the impact of our pricing and cost management initiatives. These efforts delivered a combined 280 basis points of gross margin expansion year-over-year, lifting our overall adjusted gross margin to 57.2% from 55.1% in Q2 2023. This not only exceeded our guidance but positions us well against peers like Medtronic and Stryker, who reported margins in the mid-50s amid similar industry headwinds.

Let me break this down into pricing and cost levers separately, with the quantitative impacts, then tie it to our strategic playbook in the Medical Devices space.

Pricing remains a cornerstone of our strategy, especially in a landscape shaped by payer scrutiny, bundled payments, and the shift to value-based care. We realized a 2.8% increase in core average selling prices, or ASPs, across our portfolio—our strongest quarterly lift in two years. This was driven by a multi-pronged approach.

First, product mix optimization: We leaned into higher-margin segments like our premium orthopedics and neuromodulation franchises. For instance, uptake of our EvoSpine modular spinal implants grew 15% year-over-year, commanding a 12% ASP premium over legacy systems due to superior clinical outcomes in fusion rates, backed by our Level 1 evidence from the SPINE-2023 registry. Conversely, we strategically de-emphasized low-margin commodity stents, which fell to just 8% of cardio revenue from 12% last year.

Second, contractual and reimbursement tailwinds: In the US, which represents 52% of our revenue, favorable CMS updates under the 2024 OPPS final rule boosted reimbursement for our peripheral vascular devices by an average 3.2%, allowing us to hold firm on ASPs despite commercial payer pushback. We renewed 85% of our top 20 GPO contracts with embedded escalators tied to our Outcomes360 data platform, which demonstrates 20-25% reductions in readmissions for our TAVR valves—mirroring successes seen with Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien platform.

Regionally, Europe, at 25% of revenue, faced HTA headwinds in Germany and France, where INAHTA reviews capped pricing on our neurostimulators at -1.5% year-over-year. We offset this with 4% ASP growth in premium markets like the Nordics via surgeon-led KOL adoption. In emerging markets, 23% of revenue led by China and India, volume growth of 18% more than compensated for 5-7% pricing erosion from NRDL negotiations—our NeuroPulse DBS system secured a spot on China's 2024 NRDL list at a 10% discount but with tripled volumes.

Overall, pricing contributed 150 basis points to margin expansion, adding $85 million to the quarter's gross profit—on track for our full-year target of 2-3% core ASP growth.

Complementing pricing, our cost initiatives generated $45 million in sequential quarterly savings, or $180 million annualized, representing 320 basis points of margin benefit. We've executed aggressively without compromising quality or innovation in our ISO 13485-certified facilities.

On supply chain resilience and procurement: Post-COVID, we've derisked our stack—titanium for orthopedics, 30% of COGS, costs stabilized at $25/kg after hedging 70% of 2024 needs, down from $32/kg peaks. Our VendorSync AI platform, now live across 80% of suppliers, improved demand forecasting accuracy to 95%, slashing excess inventory by 22% and obsolete stock write-offs by $12 million. This echoes Abbott's supply chain playbook but tailored to device-specific cleanroom constraints.

Manufacturing efficiencies: We completed Phase 2 of our SmartFactory automation rollout, installing cobots and IoT-enabled lines in our Galway, Ireland, and Reynosa, Mexico sites. Yield rates on our cardio rhythm management devices jumped to 98.5% from 96.2%, driving a 9% reduction in conversion costs. Site transfers from high-cost US facilities to Reynosa saved $28 million annualized, with no disruptions—FDA 483 observations at zero.

Indirect spend and R&D productivity: Overhead cuts via zero-based budgeting trimmed SG&A by 4% as a percent of revenue, including a 10% headcount optimization in non-core functions. In R&D, 18% of revenue, we rationalized our pipeline, sunsetting three Phase II programs to reallocate $50 million toward next-gen bioresorbable stents, targeting FDA breakthrough designation.

Regionally, APAC cost initiatives shone brightest: Local-for-local manufacturing in Suzhou cut logistics costs by 15% for our electrophysiology catheters, fueling 22% revenue growth there.

These initiatives aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our Margin+10 framework, aiming for 60%+ gross margins by 2026 through pricing power from clinical differentiation and costs via digital ops. In Med Devices, where raw material inflation lingers—polymers up 5% year-over-year—and biosimilars erode ortho margins, our focus on procedural enablers—like robotics integration with our ArtiGrip endoscopes—supports premium pricing. We're monitoring tariff risks in China but hedged via diversified sourcing.

Looking ahead, we expect pricing to deliver another 2.5% ASP lift in H2, with cost savings ramping to $200 million annualized. This underpins our raised FY24 gross margin guidance to 57.5-58.0% and supports 8-10% organic revenue growth.

Thank you, Alex.

Alex Rivera:
Excellent overview, Michael. Now, moving on to our gross margin trends and supply chain commentary, which ties closely into that.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Alex. I'll now turn to our gross margin performance and provide some color on supply chain dynamics, which continue to be a key focus area for us here at InnoMed Devices.

Starting with the headline: For the second quarter, our GAAP gross margin came in at 69.2%, representing a 240 basis point improvement year-over-year and 110 basis points sequentially from Q1. On a non-GAAP basis, which excludes certain amortization and restructuring charges, we delivered 71.5%, up 280 basis points year-over-year. This marks our strongest quarterly gross margin in over two years and puts us back on track toward our long-term target of 72-74% by fiscal 2026.

Let me break down the key drivers. First, favorable product mix contributed approximately 150 basis points of expansion. We saw accelerated growth in our higher-margin consumables and capital-adjacent segments, particularly in our Structural Heart franchise—think next-gen TAVR valves akin to Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien platform—and our Electrophysiology ablation catheters, which grew 28% year-over-year. These categories carry gross margins north of 80%, offsetting some softness in lower-margin capital equipment like our robotic-assisted surgical systems, where we faced competitive pricing pressures from Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci ecosystem.

Second, ASP stability and pricing discipline added about 90 basis points. In the U.S., our Medicare Advantage mix held steady at 42%, but we successfully implemented targeted price increases of 3-5% on our neuromodulation leads and spinal cord stimulators, similar to what's been executed by peers like Medtronic in their Chronic Pain portfolio. Internationally, we navigated reimbursement headwinds in Europe—Germany's NUB pricing reforms bit us by about 1.5% on orthopedics—but offset this with 4% ASP growth in Japan on our premium knee implants, bolstered by PMDA approvals for our new porous titanium coating tech.

Third, cost productivity initiatives drove the remainder, roughly 100 basis points. Our manufacturing optimization program, which we ramped up post-COVID, delivered $45 million in COGS savings this quarter. This includes yield improvements on our semiconductor-dependent wearable cardiac monitors—now at 98% from 94% a year ago—and automation of sterile packaging lines at our Galway, Ireland facility, reducing labor content by 15%. We also realized $12 million in procurement savings through our strategic sourcing alliance with DuPont for high-performance polymers used in our drug-eluting stents.

Shifting to supply chain commentary, I'm pleased to report that our resiliency efforts are yielding tangible results amid a still-challenging macro environment. Global logistics costs have eased 20% from their 2022 peaks, but inflation in raw materials—titanium up 8% year-over-year, nitinol alloys up 12%—and contract manufacturing capacity constraints persist, particularly for ethylene oxide sterilization services following EPA regulatory scrutiny.

Regionally: U.S. and North America, 65% of revenue, supply continuity is excellent, with inventory days on hand at a healthy 7.2 months, down from 8.1 prior quarter. We've dual-sourced 85% of our critical components, including MRI-compatible leads, mitigating single points of failure.

Europe, 20% of revenue: Brexit-related customs delays have normalized, but we're actively reshoring balloon catheter extrusion from Asia to our new greenfield plant in Heredia, Costa Rica, which serves EU tenders. This has reduced lead times by 40% and FX exposure.

Asia-Pacific and China, 15% of revenue: Growth here is robust at 32% year-over-year, driven by our partnership with Mindray for localized Class III approvals on our endoscopy suite. However, U.S.-China tariffs and COVID lockdowns in key sterilizer hubs like Shanghai pressured margins by 50 basis points. We've responded by qualifying three new Mexican suppliers for disposable syringes and introducing blockchain traceability for our supply ledger, cutting counterfeit risks in emerging markets.

Strategically, we're leaning into vertical integration and digital supply chain tech to sustain these gains. We've invested $150 million in a new U.S.-based semiconductor fab partnership for custom ASICs in our glucose monitoring CGMs—mirroring Dexcom's playbook—to derisk from TSMC shortages. Sustainability is also key: 45% of our titanium now comes from recycled sources via our Stryker-collaborative supply consortium, supporting EU MDR compliance and appealing to ESG-focused hospital GPOs like Vizient.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 gross margins of 70-71%, with tailwinds from mix and productivity outweighing modest FX headwinds from a stronger USD. Supply chain risks remain elevated—think Red Sea disruptions impacting 5% of ocean freight—but our scenario planning, including a +25% inventory buffer for orthobiologics, positions us well. We're confident this sets the stage for accelerated expansion as we lap easier comps and roll out our AI-optimized da Vinci competitor in H2 2025.

Alex Rivera:
Thanks, Michael, that's comprehensive. Next up is inventory management and working capital optimization—another area where you've led the charge.

Michael Chen:
Absolutely, Alex. Today, I'd like to dive deep into our inventory management and working capital optimization efforts, which have been a cornerstone of our operational excellence in the medical devices sector. As you know, in our industry—dominated by high-value, regulated products like drug-eluting stents, TAVR valves, electrophysiology catheters, and our flagship CardioFlow™ structural heart platforms—effective inventory stewardship is critical. We face unique headwinds: stringent FDA and EU MDR sterilization requirements, finite shelf lives on biologics-integrated implants, and supply chain volatility from specialized raw materials like nitinol alloys and platinum-iridium electrodes. Yet, through disciplined execution, we've delivered industry-leading results that directly bolster our free cash flow generation.

Let me start with the headline metrics, which underscore our progress. In Q2, our Days Inventory Outstanding—or DIO—improved to 92 days, down 18 days or 16% year-over-year from 110 days in Q2 2023, and a sequential improvement of 5 days from Q1. This places us at the lower end of our med device peer set—think Medtronic's cardiovascular segment or Boston Scientific's interventional cardiology lines—where the industry average hovers around 105-120 days per recent S&P Capital IQ data. Inventory turns accelerated to 4.0x for the quarter, up from 3.3x year-over-year, reflecting tighter control over our $450 million global inventory base, which declined 15% year-over-year despite 12% topline growth in our high-margin disposables like our next-gen ablation catheters.

This DIO compression directly fueled a 25-day reduction in our Cash Conversion Cycle, or CCC, to 145 days—our best in five years. For context, our Days Sales Outstanding, or DSO, held steady at 68 days, supported by enhanced AR collections amid stable Medicare reimbursement rates under the CY2025 OPPS final rule. Meanwhile, Days Payable Outstanding, or DPO, expanded modestly to 115 days through strategic vendor financing, without compromising relationships with key suppliers like our nitinol extruder partners in Costa Rica.

Turning to the technical initiatives driving these outcomes, we've leaned heavily into digital transformation. Our rollout of an AI-powered demand sensing platform, integrated with SAP S/4HANA, has been transformative. Leveraging machine learning algorithms trained on 36 months of historical procedure volume data from Vizient and Premier databases—factoring in elective PCI trends, structural heart adoption rates, and even regional CMS claims data—we've achieved 92% forecast accuracy at the SKU level for our top 80% of inventory value via ABC analysis. This has enabled a 22% reduction in safety stock levels for slow-moving orthopedic-adjacent products like our peripheral stents, while dynamically adjusting reorder points for high-velocity items such as guidewires and sheaths.

We've also scaled Vendor-Managed Inventory, or VMI, programs with 15 strategic suppliers, covering 35% of our raw materials bill. For instance, our partnership with a leading Japanese polymer fabricator for balloon catheter linings mirrors Abbott's supply chain playbook, allowing them to replenish our just-in-time hubs in Galway, Ireland, based on real-time Kanban signals from RFID-tagged bins. This has shaved 8-10 days off lead times, critical amid ongoing resin shortages echoing the 2022 supply disruptions.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positively. In the U.S., which accounts for 55% of our inventory deployment, DIO hit a stellar 85 days, buoyed by our distribution center consolidation in Memphis—now a centralized hub serving our electrophysiology growth markets. This offset softer elective procedure volumes post-respiratory season. EMEA, at 25% of inventory, improved to 98 days, thanks to MDR-compliant serialization tracking that minimized write-offs on expiring embolic coils, down 30% year-over-year. APAC remains our stretch goal at 105 days, challenged by China's NMPA localization mandates pushing 20% domestic sourcing for stents; however, our new Singapore ASI facility has cut import duties and expedited customs clearance by 40%, positioning us for 10% DIO compression in FY2025 as Volume-Based Procurement tenders stabilize.

Strategically, these efforts align with our Resilient Growth 2027 framework. We're prioritizing EOQ optimization for capital equipment spares—like components for our CardioFlow™ consoles, akin to Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci logistics—targeting a 20% inventory reduction without stockouts, even in surge scenarios like the 2023 peripheral artery disease uptick. We've also embedded ESG considerations, reducing obsolescence waste by 25% through circular economy pilots, recycling platinum from returned pacemakers in partnership with Johnson Matthey. Looking ahead, we expect Q3 DIO at 88-92 days, with CCC trending toward 135 days by fiscal year-end, generating an incremental $75 million in working capital release to fund R&D in our pulsation therapy pipeline and bolt-on M&A in neuromodulation.

In summary, our inventory and working capital discipline isn't just cost avoidance—it's a competitive moat in med devices, enabling faster innovation cycles and superior ROIC. We're proud of these results and remain committed to operational leverage as we navigate a market with 5-7% procedural growth projected by Millennium Research.

Alex Rivera:
Outstanding, Michael. Now, next, new product launches and their contribution to growth. Lena, over to you for this one, as it ties into our pipeline.

Dr. Lena Novak:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'd like to dive deeper into one of the key drivers behind our exceptional Q2 results: our new product launches and their outsized contribution to top-line growth. As you know, InnoMed Devices has long been at the forefront of innovation in the medical devices space, competing head-to-head with leaders like Medtronic, Boston Scientific, and Stryker. This quarter, our disciplined R&D investment—up 18% year-over-year to $245 million, or 12% of revenues—paid off handsomely, with new product introductions fueling 42% of our overall 15% organic revenue growth.

Let me break this down by highlighting our three major launches over the past 12 months, their performance metrics, and the strategic tailwinds positioning us for sustained momentum.

First, the CardioFlow XT Structural Heart Platform. Launched in Q4 of last year with full FDA approval and CE Mark, this next-generation transcatheter mitral valve repair system builds on the TAVR success stories from Abbott's MitraClip and Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien platforms. We've incorporated proprietary AI-driven imaging algorithms for real-time procedural guidance, reducing fluoroscopy time by 35% in our pivotal trials and improving acute success rates to 96%. In Q2 alone, CardioFlow XT generated $128 million in net sales—up 220% sequentially from Q1—accounting for 22% of our Cardiovascular segment's $580 million total, which grew 28% year-over-year. Gross margins on this platform hit 72%, well above our company average of 68%, thanks to optimized supply chain localization in our Galway, Ireland facility. Regionally, U.S. adoption has been explosive at 65% of sales, driven by strong reimbursement under the CMS NTAP pathway. In Europe, we're seeing 25% quarter-over-quarter ramps in Germany and France, while APAC—particularly China post-NMPA approval—contributed 10% with initial tenders in Shanghai hospitals. Looking ahead, we expect CardioFlow to scale to $600 million annualized run-rate by FY2025, capturing share in the $8 billion global structural heart market growing at 15% CAGR.

Second, our OrthoSense Active Implant System. Rolled out in Q1 this year, this smart orthopedic knee implant integrates embedded sensors for post-op gait analysis and remote monitoring via Bluetooth Low Energy connectivity—think of it as a Freestyle Libre for joints, akin to Zimmer Biomet's Rosa Robotics ecosystem but with always-on telemetry. Early clinical data from our 500-patient ROSA study showed a 28% reduction in 90-day readmissions, directly addressing value-based care pressures from payers like UnitedHealthcare. Q2 sales hit $95 million, representing 18% of our Orthopedics & Spine segment's 19% year-over-year growth to $520 million. Margins expanded to 70% due to high-volume titanium alloy production at our new Ankeny, Iowa plant. U.S. penetration is at 55%, bolstered by bundled payment contracts, while EMEA grew 40% year-over-year amid NICE guidelines favoring sensor-enabled devices. Emerging markets like Brazil and India added $12 million, or 13% of segment sales, via partnerships with local distributors. Strategically, this positions us to defend against DePuy Synthes' dominance, with a $1.2 billion addressable market in digital orthopedics expanding at 22% CAGR through AI-enabled predictive analytics.

Third, NeuroLink Pro Neuromodulation Array. Our latest in neuromodulation, launched last month with Breakthrough Device Designation from the FDA, this closed-loop deep brain stimulation system for Parkinson's uses machine learning to auto-adjust stimulation parameters based on real-time neural biomarkers—outpacing Medtronic's Percept RC in responsiveness by 40% per our HEADSTART trial. Though early innings, it contributed $22 million in Q2 pull-forward sales within our Neuromodulation franchise, which grew 32% year-over-year to $210 million. We project $250 million in FY2024 revenues, with 75% gross margins from our advanced ASIC chip fab in Austin, Texas.

Overall impact: Collectively, these launches drove 31% of our total $2.1 billion Q2 revenue—up from 14% a year ago—and expanded new product revenue growth to 65% year-over-year. This isn't just volume; it's high-margin, sticky revenue with 85% customer retention in launch cohorts. Technologically, our $150 million investment in digital surgery initiatives—like 5G-enabled OR integration and cloud-based registries—has de-risked adoption, mirroring Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci playbook but across modalities.

Regionally, North America remains our growth engine at 62% of new product sales (24% year-over-year), Europe at 22% (amid MDR compliance wins), and APAC/EM at 16% (doubling year-over-year on regulatory momentum). Challenges like U.S. elective procedure backlogs from respiratory seasons were offset by our 1,200-person field force expansion.

Forward-looking, our 18-product pipeline—including a robotic ablation catheter and glucose biosensors—positions us for 20-22% organic growth in FY2025, outpacing the 7% industry CAGR per Evaluate MedTech forecasts. We're leveraging M&A bolt-ons, like our recent $450 million acquisition of a peptide drug-device combo player, to accelerate into adjacencies. Risks include supply chain inflation and competitor IP disputes, but our 35% R&D-to-sales reinvestment and fortress balance sheet—$1.8 billion cash—give us conviction.

Alex Rivera:
Impressive progress, Lena. Finally, on FDA approvals and CE marks obtained—this has been transformative.

Dr. Lena Novak:
Thank you, Alex. Before we move on, let me highlight our recent FDA approvals and CE marks, which validate the technical excellence of our R&D team and unlock significant commercial upside in the $55 billion global orthopedics market, where we're targeting high-growth segments like minimally invasive spine and extremity reconstruction.

In late May, we secured FDA 510(k) clearance for our flagship OmniFlex™ Spinal Fusion System—a next-generation, expandable interbody cage with integrated bioactive coatings derived from our proprietary NanoHydroxy™ technology. This clearance builds on our IDE study data from 2023, which demonstrated a 28% reduction in subsidence rates and 35% faster fusion times compared to predicate devices like Medtronic's Prevail™ or Globus Medical's CoRoent® XL. We're projecting this product alone to drive $180 million in incremental U.S. revenue over the next 24 months, with a 45% gross margin profile at scale, fueled by our existing surgeon network of over 2,500 KOLs.

Complementing this, we received full CE Mark certification under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR)—the industry's gold standard post-2021—for both the OmniFlex system and our new ExtremiLock™ distal radius plating platform. The ExtremiLock, a low-profile, variable-angle locking plate system optimized for osteoporotic fractures, addressed the rigorous Notified Body scrutiny on our clinical endpoints, including a 22% improvement in DASH scores at 12 months from our 180-patient PMC study. This MDR-compliant portfolio positions us for immediate penetration into the €12 billion European orthopedics market, where we've already seen a 15% quarter-over-quarter increase in LOIs from top-tier hospitals like Charité in Berlin and Addenbrooke's in the UK.

Regionally, these approvals are game-changers. In the U.S., FDA clearance accelerates our launch timeline by six months, aligning perfectly with the CMS FY2025 IPPS reimbursement updates that boost DRG payments for spinal fusions by 4.2%. We've already ramped U.S. inventory to support a Q3 commercial rollout, targeting 12% market share in expandable cages within 18 months—up from our current 4% in legacy interbody devices—and chipping away at incumbents like Zimmer Biomet and DePuy Synthes, who hold 60% combined.

In Europe, the CE marks mitigate the MDR bottleneck that's plagued the industry, with over 75% of legacy devices failing recertification per recent BSI data. Our approvals under TÜV SÜD validation give us a first-mover edge in the fragmented extremity plating space, where we're forecasting €75 million in Year 1 sales, growing at 32% CAGR through 2027. We're also leveraging this momentum for parallel filings: PMDA Shonin in Japan by Q4 '24 for OmniFlex, tapping the ¥1.2 trillion Asia-Pacific spine market, and ANVISA approval in Brazil to capture emerging market tailwinds.

Strategically, these regulatory successes stem from our Pivot to Precision initiative—a $120 million, three-year R&D investment blending AI-driven finite element analysis for implant optimization and bioresorbable PEEK composites to reduce revision rates by up to 40%. We've de-risked our pipeline, advancing three more programs to pivotal stages: the FlexiCore™ motion-preserving disc (PMA submission H1 '25) and our robotic-assisted ArthroGuide™ navigation system. Partnerships are amplifying this—our co-development deal with Stryker's sales arm gives us access to 40% more ORs, while our surgeon equity program has driven 65% trial-to-commercial conversion.

Financially, these milestones contributed to Q2's 22% year-over-year revenue growth to $285 million, with regulatory-driven new product sales up 150% sequentially. We now guide FY24 orthopedics revenue to $1.25 billion—a 28% increase—with EPS expansion to $3.45, assuming no major macro headwinds. Looking ahead, our Regulatory Flywheel—approvals begetting data begetting more approvals—positions InnoMed to deliver 20-25% organic growth annually through the decade, outpacing the 6-8% industry average per Evaluate MedTech forecasts.

These FDA and CE achievements aren't just checkboxes—they're the foundation for sustainable leadership in medtech's most defensible segments.

Alex Rivera:
I will now turn the call over to Michael for a review of our financial results.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Alex. As Alex mentioned, we delivered a strong financial performance this quarter. Total revenue came in at $2.1 billion, up 15% year-over-year on an organic basis, driven by the new product momentum and procedural growth across our franchises. Adjusted EPS was $1.42, exceeding the high end of our guidance range.

Breaking it down, Cardiovascular revenue grew 28% to $580 million, Orthopedics & Spine up 19% to $520 million, and Neuromodulation up 32% to $210 million. Expenses were well-controlled: SG&A as a percent of revenue declined 4 points to 32%, reflecting our productivity gains. Operating margin expanded to 22.5%, up from 19% last year.

For full-year guidance, we're raising the bar: organic revenue growth to 12-14%, adjusted gross margins to 57.5-58%, and EPS to $5.80-$6.00, incorporating the pricing and cost tailwinds we discussed.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Dr. Lena for an update on our product pipeline.

Dr. Lena Novak:
Thank you, Michael. I'm excited to share some updates on our innovative pipeline. We recently received FDA clearance for OmniFlex™, a groundbreaking expandable interbody cage that reduces subsidence rates by 28% and accelerates fusion times, promising superior outcomes in spinal procedures.

Building on the new launches we covered, our broader pipeline includes 18 programs, with three advancing to pivotal trials, including robotic ablation tools and advanced CGMs. These position us for multi-year growth.

Now, back to Alex for Q&A.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Lena. Operator, we are now ready to take questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Instructions for asking questions: Press star then one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Thanks, good morning. Alex, Michael—impressive margin expansion. Can you elaborate more on the sustainability of the 2.8% ASP growth amid payer pressures, especially in emerging markets?

Alex Rivera:
Good question, John. Michael, your thoughts?

Michael Chen:
Sure, Alex. John, the 2.8% ASP lift was broad-based, with product mix and reimbursement tailwinds offsetting EM pricing erosion. In China, NRDL inclusion for NeuroPulse at a discount drove volume tripling, and we're targeting 2-3% full-year core ASP growth through clinical differentiation like our Outcomes360 data. Peers like Edwards have shown this model works sustainably.

Alex Rivera:
Thanks, Michael.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Hi, team. On inventory, the DIO improvement to 92 days is great—how much further can you push this without risking stockouts, given supply volatility?

Michael Chen:
Thanks, Lisa. Our AI demand sensing at 92% accuracy and VMI with 35% of suppliers give us confidence. We're targeting 88-92 days in Q3, with a 20% further reduction via EOQ optimization, mirroring peers like Medtronic. The +25% buffer for key items protects us.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Patel:
Thanks. Tom, on new product adoption—CardioFlow XT is ramping fast. What's driving the U.S. uptake, and any commercial hurdles in Europe?

Tom Hargrove:
Good morning, David. CardioFlow XT's AI imaging cut fluoro time 35%, resonating with interventionalists. U.S. NTAP reimbursement and our 1,200-person force drove 65% of sales there. In Europe, MDR compliance and GPO contracts are accelerating ramps—25% QoQ in Germany/France. No major hurdles; surgeon KOLs are converting fast.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for that insight, Tom.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Rodriguez with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Emily Rodriguez:
Hi, all. Lena, congrats on OmniFlex FDA clearance and CE marks. How does this impact the ortho pipeline timeline, and any update on Japan/PMDA?

Dr. Lena Novak:
Thanks, Emily. OmniFlex positions us for 12% share in expandable cages, with Q3 U.S. rollout. The MDR for ExtremiLock gives first-mover edge in extremities. PMDA Shonin for OmniFlex by Q4 '24 taps Asia spine growth; our Pivot to Precision has FlexiCore PMA H1 '25 on track. These flywheel effects support 20-25% ortho growth.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for your questions. Before we conclude, I want to thank our employees, customers, and partners for their continued support. We are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders.

Thank you for joining us today.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

Unlocks $180M+ US revenue, €75M Europe Year 1, 12% cage share; supports ortho growth to $1.25B FY24.
